name: PT RMK Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: RMK Energy - a Musi river coal port priced for a boom its toll book does not support
frontmatter.summary: RMK Energy runs the rail-connected Kramasan coal port, the Simpang unloading station and a private hauling road into Muara Enim, alongside a low-margin coal-trading book. The 2026 rebound is traded volume, not a step-change in port economics. At today's price the shares need the bull case, a full road ramp and high-teens margins, to be justified; the base case does not support them. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The asset is a rupiah toll, not a reserve: RMKE is paid to unload trains at Simpang, haul coal to Kramasan and load barges, and it trades coal alongside; in FY2025 barge loading was 7.95 Mt and coal sales 2.35 Mt on revenue of IDR2,216.8bn [S2, S8].

The data pack understates depreciation and the dividend: restated D&A is IDR75.7bn against the pack's near-zero line, so EBITDA is IDR398.0bn, and the FY2025 dividend the pack missed was IDR130.9bn [S2, S6].

The 2026 recovery is trading, not the port: first-half revenue rose to IDR1,592.9bn as coal sales reached 1.7 Mt, but barge loading fell to 3.2 Mt and the coal-sales segment supplied 72.1% of revenue while 63.7% of gross profit came from services [S8].

At Rp294 the equity is worth IDR6,431.2bn; our DCF at a 12.5% cost of capital gives Rp145, the base-case target is Rp156 and the probability-weighted target Rp152, a return of -46.8%. The bull case reaches Rp368, so the market is pricing most of the bull; the base case does not get there [S0, S2].

The balance sheet has re-levered: gross debt rose to IDR1,073.1bn at 30 June 2026 from IDR453.7bn at end-2025 against cash of IDR547.3bn, about a turn of EBITDA rather than net cash, and interest rises to IDR85.8bn as the Phase II bonds run for a full year [S0, S3, S8].

blocks.text: **Rating: SELL · target Rp152 · last close Rp294 · return -46.8%**

RMK Energy owns the infrastructure that moves South Sumatra coal from the train to the barge. Coal arrives by rail at the company's unloading station at Simpang, is carried a short distance to the Kramasan port on the Musi river and loaded onto barges for the voyage to the export anchorage; alongside the toll business the company buys and sells coal on its own account [S2, S8]. In FY2025 the port loaded 7.95 Mt and the trading book sold 2.35 Mt, producing revenue of IDR2,216.8bn and restated EBITDA of IDR398.0bn [S2]. The first half of 2026 changed the mix sharply: revenue reached IDR1,592.9bn, coal sales rose to 1.7 Mt, hauling-road volume reached 1.4 Mt, but barge loading fell to 3.2 Mt [S8].

The variant view is about what the equity is worth, not whether the business is good. The company describes Kramasan as the only private coal logistics complex in South Sumatra integrated with the train, with barge-loading conveyors rated at 6,000 tonnes an hour and a stockpile of 600,000 tonnes [S2, S8]. That is a genuine moat in a basin where mines are far from the river. But the earnings are a toll and a trading spread, not a commodity rent: the port earns a rupiah tariff per tonne and the trading book passes coal cost through, so revenue can multiply while gross profit barely moves [S2, S8]. In the first half the coal-sales segment was 72.1% of revenue, but 63.7% of gross profit came from the service segment, which is the asset we want to own [S8].

At Rp294 the equity is worth IDR6,431.2bn. Our DCF, at a cost of capital of 12.5% and the desk's through-cycle coal deck, gives Rp145 a share; the base-case target is Rp156 and the probability-weighted target Rp152, a return of -46.8% [S0, S2]. The bear case is Rp68 and the bull case Rp368. The price sits between the base and the bull: the market is pricing most of the case in which the road fills, margins return to the high teens and the cost of capital falls. The base case is the most likely path, and it is well below the price [S0, S2]. The market is paying a multiple of the book value of the port and the road, not a discount to the cash they generate [S0].

The balance sheet is the second disagreement. Gross debt rose to IDR1,073.1bn at 30 June 2026 from IDR453.7bn at end-2025 as the company issued its Phase II sustainable bonds, and the Phase I series A tranche of IDR116.0bn matured on 16 July 2026, just after the balance-sheet date [S2, S3, S8]. Against cash of IDR547.3bn, that is net debt of about a turn of EBITDA, not a net-cash balance sheet [S3, S8]. Interest expense rises from IDR35.5bn in FY2025 to IDR85.8bn in FY2027E on our numbers; the FY2026E P&L already carries the H1 2026 finance cost of IDR34.8bn plus a second half at the second-quarter post-bond run-rate, because the IDR600.0bn Phase II bond was issued in March 2026 [S3, S0, S8]. The refinancing terms will reset the cost of capital for the whole asset, which is why the bear case also lifts WACC [S3, S8].

Coal logistics in South Sumatra is a river business. The Musi is navigable to Palembang, and barges are the cheapest way to move coal from the basin to ocean-going vessels; ports that sit on the rail line can arbitrage the long, slow road haul. The economics are utilisation and turnaround: a port with spare capacity earns very high incremental margins on each extra tonne, while a port running at capacity must build before it can grow. A private hauling road can substitute for public roads only when it reaches the mine gate, which is why road extensions are the growth lever and why a public-road ban is a structural gift to the owner of the road.

What would change the view: barge loading returning above the FY2024 level with a stable service gross margin, the hauling road converting the identified third-party mines into contracted volume, or a coal deck that holds materially above its through-cycle marker rather than reverting to it [S2, S8, S11]. The reverse is equally clear: a national output cut that shrinks the basin's export pool, or a further rise in the trading share, would keep revenue high and profit per tonne low [S10].

RMKE operates two segments that share one coal chain. Coal services cover train unloading at Simpang, haulage to Kramasan, stockpiling and barge loading, plus the Gunung Megang loading station and heavy-equipment rental; coal trading buys coal at the mine stockpile, moves it through the same facilities and sells it to buyers on barges [S2, S8]. The segments are vertically linked: higher service volume enables higher coal-sales throughput, and higher trading demand raises service utilisation, which is why management presents them as mutually reinforcing rather than as a conglomerate discount [S8]. The economic difference matters: services supplied 63.7% of first-half gross profit while the coal-sales segment took the larger share of revenue, so the service book is the profit engine and the trading book is the volume filler [S8].

The infrastructure is the competitive position. Kramasan has three barge-loading conveyor lines, a stockpile of 600,000 tonnes and capacity that the company is upgrading to 28 Mtpa; the Simpang station has five container yards and capacity for 18 train sets a day; the Gunung Megang station, the first private train-loading system in Muara Enim, can load 14,000 tonnes a day [S8]. The dedicated hauling road is the newest asset: the 2Q 2026 presentation describes 38 km as completed and in operation since the first quarter of 2025, with a further extension planned, whereas the FY2025 annual report still described a 39 km road under construction at the balance-sheet date; we use the later operational disclosure and flag the difference [S2, S8].

The road is the growth engine because it converts road-hauled coal into port throughput and gives the company tonnes beyond the rail-linked mines. By December 2025 the company had signed three new customers, PT Menambang Muara Enim (MME), PT Wiraduta Sejahtera Langgeng (WSL) and PT Duta Bara Utama (DBU), with MME alone carrying potential volume of up to 1 Mtpa, and it had moved 1.3 Mt over the road to November 2025 against a universe of 19 potential mines in the area [S11]. The first half of 2026 shows the ramp: hauling volume reached 1.4 Mt, with the second quarter alone at 0.9 Mt [S8]. That is the strongest part of the equity story and the reason a pure port-utilisation argument understates the volume option.

The group also owns an in-house mine, PT Truba Bara Banyu Enim (TBBE), majority-held, which feeds the trading book. TBBE has proven reserves of 75 Mt, resources of 148.3 Mt, a stripping ratio of 4.0 and coal grading between 3,000 and 4,200 kcal/kg GAR [S8]. The company estimates the mine contributes an average of 20.0% of consolidated revenue, and TBBE coal moves through the same train, station and port as third-party tonnes [S2]. The mine's rent is therefore already inside the trading gross profit that the DCF capitalises in every forecast year and in the terminal value, and the reserve life exceeds the DCF horizon; a separate reserve NAV added on top of the trading book would double count the same tonnes. We value TBBE through the trading book and do not add a second reserve value [S2, S8].

Control sits with the founding family. PT RMK Investama holds 56.8% of the shares, Tony Saputra and the two other family directors hold small direct stakes alongside a public float of 40.7%, and the family supplies the President Commissioner and the President Director [S2, S8]. The board has five directors and three commissioners, two of them independent [S8]. The company listed in 2021, has paid a cash dividend every year since 2023, and has no rights issue since listing [S2]. It is the largest private coal logistics provider in South Sumatra by its own description, a challenger to the state-backed rail-and-port complex rather than the incumbent [S8].

Indonesia produced 790 Mt of coal in FY2025, of which 514 Mt was exported and 254 Mt went to the domestic market under the DMO at a 32.0% share [S2, S10]. The country supplies about 43.0% of a global seaborne trade of roughly 1,300 Mt, which is the source of the policy problem: the government believes Indonesian supply is large enough to depress the global price and has said it will cut national output to about 600 Mt in 2026 through the RKAB quota process [S10]. For a logistics provider the cut is double-edged. It supports the coal price and therefore the trading spread, but it reduces the tonnes available to move, and RMKE's first-half barge loading already fell to 3.2 Mt against a weak prior year [S8, S10].

The price marker is set monthly by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. The August 2026 first-period HBA for 6,322 kcal GAR coal was USD 124.44 a tonne, above the prior-year period's USD 102.22, and HBA I for 5,300 kcal coal was USD 93.27, up 3.75% [S9]. RMKE's own coal is much lower grade: the trading book sold at an average of 680,300 rupiah a tonne in the first half, a low-CV realisation that sits well below HBA III for 3,400 kcal coal at US$45.5/t, and domestic-power tonnes are capped by the DMO price of US$70.0/t [S8, S9, coal deck]. The desk's coal deck is deliberately below spot: newc is marked at US$150/t spot against US$118/t for FY2027E, HBA at US$127/t spot against US$112/t for FY2027E, and Brent at US$104/bbl spot against US$84.0/bbl for FY2027E [S0]. The HBA II and HBA III series carry spot prints but no forecast path, so they cannot drive a DCF; the model uses the reviewed newc/HBA series for the percentage change in the cost link, whose level cancels against the base year, while the report prices the trading book off the low-CV HBA III marker [S9, coal deck]. The marker is the revenue and realisation anchor, not the source of the discount: because the cost link cancels its level against the base year, it reaches the value mainly through the unpassed-cost gross-up, where the lower newc path shrinks the gross-up and lifts the modelled service margin [S0, S2, coal deck]. The gap to the market price is the 12.5% cost of capital, the 5.0% base growth path and the thin trading mix, not the marker level; the reverse DCF solves today's price on the growth axis at about 16.6%, above the bull's own revenue path [S0].

South Sumatra is the second-largest reserve basin in the country, with 8,900 Mt of reserves, more than a quarter of the national total, and it contributes only about a tenth of production, a reserve-to-output ratio that implies decades of future tonnes [S8]. PT Bukit Asam controls about 60.0% of the reserves and produced around 42 Mt in 2024, with a stated ambition to double output by 2030, supported by rail and terminal expansion [S8]. The other producers in the Lahat-Muara Enim corridor include Pendopo Energi Batubara, Mustika Indah Permai, Bumi Sekundang Enim Energi, Dizamatra Powerindo and Manambang Muara Enim, many of them not connected to the rail line, which is exactly the customer pool the hauling road is built for [S8, S11].

Regulation is the live driver. The South Sumatra governor's instruction banning coal transport on public roads, in force from the start of 2026, makes a private dedicated road the only compliant route for affected mines [S8]. At the same time PT KAI is expanding the South Sumatra coal rail network: it plans triple-track lines, is buying new locomotives and wagons that the company says will add about 28 Mtpa of coal-transport capacity, and targets 165 Mtpa of loading-terminal capacity by 2029 [S8]. The rail expansion is a volume tailwind for Simpang and Kramasan, but it also strengthens the state-linked alternative route to Tarahan and raises the question of whether the basin's logistics rent is competed away over time [S8].

The competitive map is narrow. Rail haulage on the corridor costs 806 rupiah per tonne-km, and Kramasan is the closest private port to the Tanjung Enim mines, while Tarahan is a much longer rail haul and Keramasan is a future port rather than an operating competitor [S8]. RMKE handles 7.95 Mt of barge loading against a port capacity it is upgrading to 28 Mtpa, so utilisation is the swing variable: spare capacity gives very high incremental margins on new tonnes, but the company must fill the port before the fixed-cost base earns its keep [S2, S8]. Market share at national level is small, about a percentage point of production, but in the rail-linked private segment it is the leader, and the hauling road extends that position into mines that were previously road-bound [S2, S8].

The moat is location and capital intensity, not a licence. The barriers are the rail spur, the conveyors, the port permits, the environmental approvals and the road rights; a new entrant would have to replicate a rail-connected port and a dedicated road before winning a single tonne [S2, S8]. The five forces are favourable on new entry and substitution for rail-linked mines, and less favourable elsewhere. Buyer power is concentrated: the largest customer receivable is IDR145.6bn and the top customers are large miners who can build or direct tonnes to their own facilities [S3]. Supplier power sits with KAI, which carries the coal and is also a payable of IDR19.0bn, and with Pertamina for diesel [S3, S8]. Rivalry is moderate today but rises with the KAI expansion, and the trading book competes with every other South Sumatra trader, which is why its gross margin is thin [S2, S8].

External influences run through four channels. Weather is the first: heavy rain cuts mine output, and the annual report names it as a material operational risk [S2]. Coal price is the second: it sets the trading revenue per tonne and the value of marginal mine output, while the port tariff is a rupiah service fee that resets with a lag [S2, S8]. Diesel is the third: the fleet burns 0.81 litres per tonne loaded, so a Brent move reaches hauling cost faster than the tariff resets [S2]. Policy is the fourth: RKAB quotas, the DMO, royalty rates and the public-road ban all change the volume and the rent in the same basin at the same time [S8, S10].

The history is a shrinking commodity-linked book before the 2026 rebound. Revenue fell from IDR2,733.6bn in FY2022 to IDR2,216.8bn in FY2025, gross profit from IDR588.6bn to IDR405.4bn, EBITDA from IDR533.4bn to IDR398.0bn, and net profit attributable to shareholders from IDR389.0bn to IDR241.8bn [S2]. The FY2025 decline was volume-led: barge loading fell to 7.95 Mt from 9.03 Mt and coal sales to 2.35 Mt from 2.81 Mt, so revenue fell and cost of revenue fell to IDR1,811.4bn, leaving a gross margin of 18.3%; the FY2024 comparatives come from the prior annual report [S2]. The FY2024 volume base is from the same prior-year filing [S4]. The reported profit line is cleaner than the data pack suggests: depreciation was IDR75.7bn in FY2025 and IDR78.4bn in FY2024, so EBITDA is IDR398.0bn and IDR458.7bn respectively, not the near-zero-D&A figures in the pack; we restate both years from the filings [S2, S4].

The FY2025 cost base is dominated by coal purchases because the trading book is large. Coal sales were 62.2% of FY2025 revenue, so coal purchase cost is roughly three-quarters of the IDR1,811.4bn cost of revenue, with fuel, rail freight, labour, depreciation and port costs making up the balance [S2]. Diesel use was 6,430,566 litres at 0.81 litres per tonne loaded, and the G&A line was IDR83.1bn, a little over three percent of revenue [S2]. The company missed its own FY2025 revenue target badly: it realised 57.1% of an IDR3,880.0bn target, which is a useful caution when management speaks about the next year's plan [S2].

The first half of 2026 is the other side of the cycle. Revenue was IDR1,592.9bn against IDR267.1bn of gross profit, EBITDA of IDR257.1bn and net profit of IDR163.1bn, with operating cash flow of IDR140.3bn [S8]. The mix explains the margin: coal sales were 1.7 Mt at an average price of 680,300 rupiah a tonne, while barge loading was 3.2 Mt and hauling volume 1.4 Mt [S8]. The second quarter accelerated: net profit was IDR107.3bn, average selling price 749,300 rupiah a tonne, and the company attributed the momentum to domestic coal sales and price strength rather than to a port volume recovery [S8]. That is the key distinction for valuation: the revenue recovery is real, but it sits in the segment that earns a thin spread.

The segment split makes the two books explicit. In the first half coal sales produced IDR1,148.9bn of revenue and IDR97.0bn of gross profit, while services produced IDR444.0bn of revenue and IDR170.1bn of gross profit [S8]. The service book is less than a third of revenue but the clear majority of gross profit, and the trading book is the reverse: a large revenue base earned at a thin gross margin. Our forecast therefore does not extrapolate the trading revenue line. It builds revenue from the two paths: trading revenue is held roughly flat because a mid-single-digit volume gain from the H1 run-rate offsets the lower HBA marker in the desk's FY2027E path, while service revenue grows by the high teens as the road ramps; on the first-half revenue split that weighted build is the 5.0% we use for FY2027E [S8, S9, S11]. FY2028E to FY2030E continue the same mix shift, with service volume growing toward the FY2024 port level of 9.03 Mt and trading volume growing more slowly than the marker de-rates [S8, S11].

Our forecast carries the first-half run-rate into FY2026E revenue of IDR3,185.5bn, a 43.7% increase, then slows to 5.0% in FY2027E on the weighted trading/service build above [S0, S2, S8]. Gross profit rises to IDR536.3bn and EBITDA to IDR545.9bn, a margin of 17.1% that is broadly the H1 actual once the higher-margin service mix is allowed for [S8]. From FY2027E the mix improves as trading revenue per tonne falls with the coal price and the hauling-road tonnes carry the service book, lifting the EBITDA margin to 17.7% and 18.2% by FY2030E [S0, S2]. Net profit attributable to shareholders reaches IDR290.2bn and EPS 13.3, with DPS of 3.98 at the normalised payout; FY2026E earnings already include the full H1 finance-cost run-rate and the higher interest on the Phase II stack [S0, S3, S8].

Cash conversion is not the problem. Across the three audited years the accruals ratio — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — stays well inside the ten-percent flag, with no year in which profit ran ahead of cash by a material margin [S2, S4].

| Accruals screen | FY2023A | FY2024A | FY2025A | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Net profit | IDR308.9bn | IDR272.5bn | IDR245.4bn | | Operating cash flow | IDR187.4bn | IDR422.3bn | IDR235.1bn | | Total assets at year-end | IDR2,247.7bn | IDR2,369.2bn | IDR2,840.3bn |

The FY2023 ratio uses the FY2022 year-end asset base of IDR1,676.8bn [S4]. The first half of 2026 produced IDR140.3bn of operating cash flow on IDR163.1bn of net profit, again a low accrual gap [S8]. The cash flow is absorbed by capex and dividends rather than by working capital: FY2025 capex was IDR234.1bn, the FY2025 dividend was IDR130.9bn, and the company also spent IDR44.6bn on the buyback in the first half [S2, S3, S8].

Working capital carries a governance flag, and the pack's opening line overstates the operating need. The pack's working-capital line was IDR671.2bn at end-FY2025, but that balance includes related-party items that are not operating: other receivables from related parties were IDR294.0bn at 30 June 2026, described in the notes as mainly advanced payment of expenses between parties under common control [S3]. On the operating definition, trade receivables of IDR626.1bn plus inventory of IDR28.3bn less trade payables of IDR285.0bn and the related-party payable leave annualised operating working capital at the 11.0% we use, a little above the FY2025 operating ratio on the same definition once the non-operating balances are stripped out [S2, S3]. Moving to the operating ratio takes the FY2026E balance to IDR350.4bn from the pack's IDR671.2bn, releasing the related-party and other non-operating balances once, at book; that is why the receivable is not valued a second time on top of the cash flow [S3]. Trade receivables were IDR145.6bn from the largest customer alone, and the customer list is concentrated in a handful of South Sumatra miners [S3].

The balance sheet has re-levered. Gross debt was IDR453.7bn at end-FY2025 and IDR1,073.1bn at 30 June 2026, against cash of IDR547.3bn, taking the debt-to-equity ratio to 0.55 [S3, S8]. The debt is mostly bonds: the Phase I issue included a IDR116.0bn series A tranche that matured on 16 July 2026 and a series B tranche at an 8.8% coupon, while the March 2026 Phase II issue raised IDR600.0bn in a IDR450.0bn five-year series A at 7.8% and a longer series B [S2, S3, S8]. Interest expense was IDR35.5bn in FY2025 and rises to IDR85.8bn in FY2027E on a full year of the new stack, partly offset by interest income on the cash balance [S0]. The FY2026E model line of IDR36.3bn charges opening debt only; the H1 2026 finance cost of IDR34.8bn plus a second half at the second-quarter post-bond run-rate is higher, and the gap is charged in other non-operating items so that FY2026E PBT and EPS reflect the actual stack [S3, S0]. On the 30 June balance sheet, gross debt of IDR1,073.1bn less cash of IDR547.3bn is about a turn of EBITDA; the forecast cash line is not a liquidity forecast and the valuation uses the 30 June net debt [S3, S8].

Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly but procyclical. The company paid IDR30.6bn out of FY2023 profit, 5.6% of FY2024 profit, and then IDR130.9bn, or just over half of FY2025 profit, as the FY2025 dividend, declared after the annual report was published [S2, S6]. That latest payout was a one-year step-up, not a stated policy: the record is a tenth of FY2023 profit and a low single-digit percentage of FY2024 profit, so we normalise the forward payout to 30.0% for DPS and the dividend-capacity statement [S2, S6]. It also announced a buyback of up to IDR200.0bn in January 2026 and had spent IDR44.6bn by June [S7, S8], and it is investing IDR45.5bn in electric heavy equipment and a dedicated substation as part of its electrification plan [S8]. Paying a large dividend while raising debt for the hauling road and the fleet is a choice we would test if the coal price falls: the dividend is the market's anchor, but it is also the first line that would have to be cut if the trading spread compresses [S2, S6].

Earnings quality: the accruals ratio is not alarming, cash conversion is positive, and the FY2025 audit opinion is unqualified, signed by KAP Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra [S2]. The flags are optics-class rather than manipulation-class. The pack's D&A and dividend are wrong, and we have restated them [S2, S6]. Related-party balances are material: IDR294.0bn of other receivables and IDR18.4bn of trade payables at 30 June 2026, both disclosed and explained as common-control advances [S3]. The customer concentration in receivables is the other watch item, with the largest single customer at IDR145.6bn [S3]. None of these points to fictitious revenue; all of them point to a controlled company where the minority shareholder depends on the controller's stewardship.

The method set fits a toll infrastructure asset rather than a miner. The port, the unloading station and the hauling road are long-lived, contracted by use rather than by reserve, and their cash flow is a rupiah tariff plus a trading spread; a DCF on the port and road at the desk's through-cycle coal deck is therefore the right primary frame, and a current-year multiple on a trading-inflated revenue base would mislead [S2, S8]. We give the DCF the dominant weight, set EV/EBITDA to zero because the peer data packs are not D&A-restated and would mix definitions across leased and owned fleets, and keep a small P/BV cross-check that now sits below the DCF, so it does not lift the target [S0, S2]. The absence of an EV/EBITDA cross-check is a deliberate choice, not an omission: the listed coal-logistics peers range from a distressed trader to a niche fleet operator, and their reported EBITDA is not comparable without the same restatement we have applied to RMKE [S0]. The service and trading books are not separated inside the DCF, but the revenue path is built from their two margins and the report shows the segment gross profit; a single growth rate would blur them, which is why the build, not the schema, carries the distinction [S8].

The cost of capital is 12.53%. The cost of equity starts from the 7.45% ten-year rupiah government yield, less the 1.62% Indonesia sovereign default spread that the Damodaran build strips out to reach the relevant rupiah risk-free rate, plus a levered beta of 1.13 applied to the sum of the 4.23% mature-market equity premium and the 2.46% Indonesia country premium. That is 7.45% less 1.62%, plus 1.13 times the sum of the two premiums, giving a cost of equity of 13.39% [house macro deck]. The pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC is the house build of the 7.45% rupiah yield plus a corporate spread, 9.45%, on the bond-heavy stack, entering at one minus the 22.00% tax rate, with equity at 85.70% and debt at 14.30% of the capital structure [house macro deck]. The interest forecast uses a separate 8.0% input, the contractual coupon stack we judge will actually be paid; the two rates are deliberate and measure different things, the WACC charging a market spread on the debt and the P&L the coupon on the drawn stack. Using the lower contractual rate in the WACC as well would cut the cost of capital and lift the DCF, so the valuation is conservative on this input rather than aggressive [S3, house macro deck]. The beta is the industry default and may understate the risk of a small-cap coal logistics name with a concentrated customer base, which is one reason we are comfortable with a cost of capital at the top of the plausible range [config]. Terminal growth is 3.2%, below nominal GDP, reflecting a mature port and road network rather than a growing commodity rent [S2, house macro deck].

The DCF gives Rp145 a share and an enterprise value of IDR3,652.1bn, of which the terminal value is 41.1% [S0]. The key drivers are the revenue path from IDR3,185.5bn in FY2026E to IDR3,983.4bn in FY2030E, a gross margin of 17.9%, capex at 7.0% of revenue in FY2026E normalising to maintenance plus growth at 5.3% of revenue, operating working capital at 11.0% of revenue, and the house rupiah terminal growth rate of 3.2% [S0, S2, S3, S8]. The capex normalisation is the change the red team was right about: the 38 km road is built, D&A is 3.3% of revenue, and holding capex flat in perpetuity against 3.2% growth implied perpetual net reinvestment and depressed the terminal value [S2, S4, S8]. The DCF value is sensitive to the coal deck through the trading spread and to WACC through the long terminal tail; the sensitivity table below shows the range, and the base value remains far below today's price even at the more favourable WACC/growth corners [S0].

The move from enterprise value to equity value is explicit and counted once. The enterprise value less net debt and minority interests gives the DCF equity value; the PT Bahtera Mustika Mulia associate is already carried on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet as an investment of IDR58.3bn, and the engine reads that line once into the equity value, so we add no separate bridge item for it [S3]. An earlier draft also added the same balance as a valuation bridge item, which double counted it; removing that item lowers the DCF value per share and every target in this report, and the figures shown here are the single-count result [S3]. TBBE is the other asset we deliberately do not add, because its rent is inside the trading gross profit the DCF capitalises [S2, S8].

The P/BV cross-check gives Rp104, -28.1% versus the DCF, so it now sits below the primary method and does not lift the target [S0]. The cross-check uses the peer median of three names and a book that still carries the IDR294.0bn related-party receivable and the revalued asset base; adjusted for the receivable, the book value would be lower still, which is why we keep its weight at ten percent and do not present it as a floor [S0, S3]. The market's own multiples make the same point from the other side: the shares trade on 26.6x FY2025 earnings, 16.7x EV/EBITDA and 3.3x book value, with a dividend yield of 2.0% [S0]. A dividend-yield anchor at that level does not compensate for a cost of equity of 13.4%.

The sensitivity grid is the cleanest statement of the variant view. Across a one-point range in WACC either way and a one-point range in terminal growth, the DCF value never reaches the market price; the base value stays far below it even at the most favourable corner [S0]. The bull scenario, which adds eight points of revenue growth every year, three points of gross margin and a one-point lower WACC, is the only path that reaches the price, at Rp368 [S0, S2]. To justify Rp294 the market must believe the road fills toward the FY2024 port level of 9.03 Mt within a year, the service margin returns to the high teens and the refinancing lowers the cost of capital, all at once. None of those is impossible; none is the most likely path, and the base case in this report is the most likely path [S2, S8].

Spot-price cross-check. The method card asks for NAV at the spot coal print alongside the through-cycle value. The desk marks newc at US$150/t and HBA at US$127/t against US$118/t and US$112/t for FY2027E [S0]. Because the trading book passes the great majority of a cargo-price move through to the buyer, a spot-price run moves the unpassed cost gross-up against the service book rather than lifting DCF revenue; the effect is roughly the lower-margin column of the sensitivity grid, where the value per share sits below the base case and far below the market price [S0, S2]. The spot-coal NAV does not rescue the rating: SELL holds on either marker [S0, S2].

What today's price implies: the reverse DCF solves the observed price on the revenue-growth axis at an implied FY2027E growth rate of 16.6%, above the bull's own revenue path, before any help from margin or the cost of capital [S0]. The market capitalisation of IDR6,431.2bn is roughly twice the DCF equity value implied by our Rp145 a share — the enterprise value of IDR3,652.1bn less net debt and minority interests, with the associate already inside the balance-sheet investment line — so the equity bridge does not close the gap [S0, S3]. The market is paying for the bull path and more: the road at the FY2024 port level, a high-teens service margin and a lower cost of capital. We would revisit the rating if the price fell towards the sensitivity grid's upper corner or if the hauling-road volumes converted into a service earnings base that our deck-consistent DCF can capitalise [S2, S8].

The downside risks, with likelihood and impact. Regulatory: a national output cut to the RKAB target would shrink the export pool and could idle marginal mine tonnes (high likelihood, high impact) [S10]. Coal price: a fall towards the desk's through-cycle marker cuts trading revenue per tonne and can slow marginal output, while the port tariff resets with a lag (high, high) [S0, S2]. Refinancing: the Phase I series A tranche has matured and the Phase II bonds reset the interest bill, so a higher-for-longer rupiah rate raises the charge on a larger debt stack (high, medium) [S3, S8]. Operational: heavy rain, rail disruption or a road closure can interrupt the chain, and the annual report names weather as a material risk (medium, medium) [S2]. Governance: the controlling family, the related-party receivable and the trading suspension of 2025 are all real features of the equity (medium, high) [S2, S3]. Liquidity: the shares were suspended for 8 trading days in 2025 as a cooling-down measure, and the free float is only 40.7%, so entry and exit can be costly in stress (medium, medium) [S2, S8].

The base case assumes the port returns towards its FY2024 throughput over the forecast years and the trading book holds its spread at the deck price; the bear and bull shock the same three drivers in mirror image: revenue growth, gross margin and the cost of capital [S2, S8]. The bear value is Rp68, the base Rp156 and the bull Rp368, with probabilities of 40.0%, 45.0% and 15.0% respectively [S0]. The bear is the output-cut case: the government's plan to cut national output to about 600 Mt from 790 Mt is implemented, barge loading falls back from an H1 2026 run-rate that was already below the prior year, the hauling-road ramp stalls at the three signed customers, the service margin compresses and the refinancing adds a point to WACC [S8, S10]. The shock is applied to the revenue-growth rate, not to a separate volume line: it removes part of the FY2026E growth, so FY2026E revenue still rises on the H1 run-rate, and the shortfall compounds from FY2027E, which is what drives the bear value down to Rp68 [S0, S8]. The bull assumes coal prices hold above the deck, barge loading returns to the FY2024 port level of 9.03 Mt within a year, the road converts MME's up-to-1 Mtpa and the 19-mine universe into service volume, the margin returns to the high teens and the cost of capital falls [S8, S11]. The base carries the largest weight because it reproduces the last actual and the company's plan, and the bear weight sits just behind it because the output cut is the report's own high-likelihood risk; the bull needs three conditions to coincide [S10, S2].

The signposts that would change the view are specific. Barge loading returning above the FY2024 level of 9.03 Mt on an annualised basis would show that the port, not the trading book, is growing [S2, S8]. The hauling road reaching the contracted MME, WSL and DBU volumes, with MME alone at up to 1 Mtpa, would add service gross profit at the high margin the first half already demonstrates [S8, S11]. The RKAB 2027 decision, the monthly HBA prints and the newc marker are the policy and price signposts [S9, S10]. On the downside, a rising trading share of revenue with a falling gross margin, or a further build in the related-party receivable, would confirm that the revenue growth is not translating into value [S3, S8].

The honest bull case is that we are wrong about the durability of the trading spread. If the domestic coal market stays tight and RMKE's trading book can grow volume without compressing margin, the revenue base grows, the service segment's fixed costs leverage and the road fills; the bull value of Rp368 is above today's price, so the market is pricing most of this path rather than rejecting it [S0, S8]. The honest bear case is that the output cut reduces basin volume, the coal price falls, and the company is left with a leveraged balance sheet, a larger interest bill and a port with spare capacity; the bear value of Rp68 is less than half the base [S0, S10]. The probability weight on the bear is close to the base because the hauling road and the public-road ban are real, sourced structural changes, but they are not enough to offset a high-likelihood output cut and a trading book whose durability is unproven; the base keeps the largest weight as the most probable path [S8, S10, S11].

Ownership and control are concentrated. PT RMK Investama holds 56.8%, the founding family directors hold small direct stakes, the public holds 40.7% and treasury stock is a fraction of the register after the buyback [S2, S8]. The family supplies the President Commissioner and the President Director, and the board has five directors and three commissioners, two of them independent [S8]. We found no disclosure of a pledge of the controlling block in the annual report, and no rights issue since the IPO; the controlling stake is large enough that a margin call on a pledge would be a supply event, so we monitor it [S2]. The free float is above the IDX minimum, but the effective tradable float is thinner than the headline because the family and the controller dominate the register [S8].

The audit and the related-party ledger are the two governance facts that matter. The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from KAP Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra, and the auditor's report is included in the annual report [S2]. Related-party other receivables were IDR294.0bn at 30 June 2026 and trade payables to related parties IDR18.4bn, both disclosed in the notes and explained as common-control advances [S3]. The company also owes KAI IDR19.0bn in trade payables, which is an operating relationship rather than a related-party one [S3]. On the operating base the related-party other receivable is just under a tenth of annualised first-half revenue, and the related-party payables a smaller share [S3]. On the IDX regime checks, neither the FY2025 annual report nor the 30 June 2026 LK discloses a special-monitoring-board designation or a B/E/L/M/S special notation [S2, S3]. We classify the related-party balances as optics-class: disclosed, stable, and not evidence of fabricated revenue, but large enough relative to equity to keep the governance discount in the bear case and to watch [S3].

The dividend record is good but young. The company paid IDR30.6bn out of FY2023 profit, 5.6% of FY2024 profit, and IDR130.9bn, or just over half of FY2025 profit, in the most recent cycle [S2] [S6]. The latest step-up was not described as a policy: the filing says only that the dividend reflects appreciation amid industry challenges, so we treat it as a one-year distribution and normalise the forward payout to 30.0% [S6]. At the FY2025 actual payout the trailing yield was 2.0%; at our normalised payout the FY2026E yield is 1.4%, neither of which compensates for the cost of equity [S0]. The step-up coincided with the bond issuance and the buyback, which is a mixed signal: it returns cash to shareholders while the company borrows for capex, and it makes the dividend sensitive to the coal price [S2, S3]. The buyback of up to IDR200.0bn announced in January 2026 is a second capital-return channel, and the IDR44.6bn executed by June shows the board is using it [S7, S8]. The shares were suspended for 8 trading days in 2025 as a cooling-down measure after a violent price move, which is not evidence of misconduct but does point to a thin, retail-driven float [S2].

ESG exposure is operational and transition-related. The company reports diesel intensity of 0.81 litres per tonne loaded, 6,430,566 litres of fuel use in FY2025 and 676,786 kWh of electricity, and it has installed telescopic chutes, fogging systems and water sprayers to control coal dust at Kramasan [S2]. The electrification programme is real: electricity use reached 2,100,000 kWh in the first half of 2026 as the substation came online, and the company is spending IDR45.5bn on electric dump trucks, a reach stacker and a forklift [S8]. The main transition risk is demand for thermal coal, which is a risk to volume rather than to the port's licence; the port would still handle coal in a declining market, but at lower throughput and with a shorter asset life than the DCF assumes [S2].

The dated catalysts are the third-quarter 2026 LK in November 2026, the RKAB 2027 quota decision around the turn of the year, the FY2026 audit and AGM dividend in early 2027, the hauling-road third-party volume ramp through 2027 and the Phase I series B maturity in mid-2028 [S2, S3, S6, S8, S10]. The Q3 LK is the first test of whether the second-quarter trading momentum persisted and whether barge loading recovered from the first-half decline [S3, S8]. The RKAB decision is the policy test: a national cut to the target would reduce the export pool but support the price, and the net effect on RMKE depends on whether its mine customers are quota-constrained [S10].

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs: barge loading volume against the FY2024 level, hauling-road volume and the customer count, coal-sales volume and the average selling price, service gross profit per tonne, the trading share of revenue, net debt and the interest charge, and the related-party receivable [S2, S3, S8]. On the price side we watch the monthly HBA prints and the desk's newc marker, because the trading spread and the through-cycle valuation both key off them [S9, S0]. A return of barge loading to the FY2024 level with a stable service margin would be the clearest evidence that the base case is too low; a further rise in the trading share with a falling gross margin would be the clearest evidence that it is too high [S2, S8].

bear.narrative: The government's plan to cut national output to about 600 Mt from 790 Mt is implemented and South Sumatra mine customers lose quota, so the growth rate runs eight points below the base path: FY2026E revenue still rises on the H1 2026 run-rate, but the shortfall compounds from FY2027E as trading volume stalls and the hauling-road ramp at three customers does not add enough service volume. The service gross margin compresses three points as fixed port costs are spread over fewer tonnes, and the Phase I series A refinancing and the larger bond stack add a percentage point to the cost of capital.

bull.narrative: Coal prices hold above the deck as export demand stays firm, the public-road ban pushes the remaining Muara Enim mines onto the private road, barge loading returns to the port's 9 Mt level within a year and the completed 38 km road converts the MME contract of up to 1 Mtpa and the 19-mine universe into service volume, lifting logistics revenue and restoring the gross margin to the high teens; the refinancing is done at a lower spread, cutting the cost of capital.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: First-half 2026 revenue was Rp1,592.9bn against Rp575.7bn in first-half 2025: coal sales supplied Rp1,148.9bn and services Rp444.0bn (S8 pp.35, S0 quarterly, S3). Annualising the run-rate gives the FY2026E +43.7% on FY2025, but the forecast is built bottom-up thereafter. FY2027E +5% is the weighted result of two paths: trading revenue roughly flat, because a 5% volume gain (H1 2026 coal sales 1.7 Mt already annualise above FY2025's 2.35 Mt, S8 p.33, S2 p.19) offsets the roughly 5% lower HBA marker in the desk's FY2027E path (S9, coal deck), and service revenue +18% as the 38 km hauling road ramps toward the MME volume of up to 1 Mtpa and the 19-mine universe (S8 p.20, S11). At the 72.1%/27.9% revenue split that is 0.72 x 0 + 0.28 x 18% = +5%. FY2028E-30E at +7%, +6%, +5% carry the same build: service volume grows toward the 9 Mt port level as the road adds customers, trading volume grows more slowly than the coal price marker de-rates, and the mix shifts toward services. No default volume haircut: FY2025's 7.95 Mt barge loading was 88% of the 9.03 Mt the port loaded in FY2024 (S2, S4), H1 2026 hauling volume grew 424.9% (S8 p.31), and 2H26 management guidance is constructive on the RKAB completion (S8 p.32).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 18.29% (Rp405.4bn on Rp2,216.8bn, S2 p.245) at deck input costs. H1 2026 ran at 16.8% (Rp267.1bn on Rp1,592.9bn, S8 p.36) because the low-margin coal-trading share rose to 72.1% of revenue (S8 p.35); that mix dilution is an actual, not a haircut, so the FY2026E input is set so the modelled margin after the coal and Brent cost links is 16.8%, matching the H1 actual. The input is 16.8% at FY2025 deck prices, but the engine grosses up COGS by the unpassed share of the coal and diesel moves (link1 0.73 x 0.10, link2 0.055 x 0.50) when newc and Brent sit above their FY2025 base, so the FY2026E input is 19.3%. As the coal deck normalises (newc 118.0 in FY2027E against a 150.35 spot) trading revenue per tonne falls and the higher-margin port and hauling book regains share, lifting the modelled margin to about 17.5% in FY2027E and 18.0% from FY2028E; the long-run 18.0% input allows for the trading book remaining a larger part of the mix than in FY2025.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal purchases are the largest cost line because 62.21% of FY2025 revenue was coal sales (S2 p.96). At the FY2025 coal-sales revenue of about Rp1,379bn and a trading gross margin in the low single digits, coal purchase cost is roughly Rp1,320bn of the Rp1,811bn cost of revenue, or 73%. Set 0.73; the port and rail-hauling cost base (fuel, labour, rail freight, depreciation) is the remaining 27%.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The trading book prices each cargo off the prevailing coal marker, so a coal-price move is largely passed to the buyer with a stable rupiah margin per tonne; the FY2025 gross margin held at 18.3% through a falling price year (S2 p.245). Set 0.90, leaving a tenth of the move in the margin as inventory and timing risk.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: FY2025 diesel use was 6.43m litres (S2 p.10), at 0.81 litres per tonne loaded (S2 p.36). At roughly Rp15,000/litre that is about Rp96bn, 5.3% of the Rp1,811bn cost of revenue. Set 0.055.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Port and hauling tariffs reset periodically against fuel, not continuously, so within a year about half of a diesel move is recovered. Set 0.50; the lag is a margin timing item, not a permanent loss, and is the reason the bear case does not also cut the pass-through.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative expense was Rp82.4bn in FY2025, 3.72% of revenue (S2 p.245), and Rp21.8bn in Q1 2026 plus Rp22.9bn in Q2 2026, 2.82% of H1 revenue (S0 quarterly). The line is people and premises and does not scale with the trading book, so we hold the lower 3.0% observed in 2026 rather than the FY2025 ratio.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated depreciation is Rp75.7bn in FY2025 and Rp78.4bn in FY2024 (S2 p.105, S4 p.99), against the data pack's Rp1.9bn and Rp2.4bn, which capture only a small G&A line. On revenue that is 3.42% and 3.19%; we hold 3.3% as the port and hauling assets grow with capex.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash capex on property, equipment and right-of-use assets was Rp234.1bn in FY2025, 10.56% of revenue, and Rp114.3bn in FY2024 (S2 p.247); H1 2026 investment cash outflow was Rp102.9bn on Rp1,592.9bn of revenue, 6.5%, and the 38 km hauling road is completed and in operation (S3 p.8, S8 p.20). The build-out is therefore behind the peak. Terminal capex should equal maintenance plus growth: D&A is 3.3% of revenue (Rp75.7bn FY2025, S2 p.105; Rp78.4bn FY2024, S4 p.99) and growth needs g x PPE/revenue = 3.25% x 0.62 = 2.0% of revenue, for about 5.3%. We taper capex from 7.0% in FY2026E (the port-upgrade and road-extension tail) to the 5.3% normalised rate by FY2029E and hold it in the terminal value, so the model no longer assumes perpetual net reinvestment of 4.7% of revenue against 3.25% growth.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is trade receivables plus inventory less trade payables: trade receivables were Rp626.1bn, inventory Rp28.3bn and trade payables Rp303.4bn at 30 June 2026, a net Rp351.0bn or 11.0% of annualised revenue (S3 notes 7, 9, 16; S0), while FY2025 on the same definition was Rp523.0bn + Rp48.1bn - Rp341.4bn = Rp229.7bn, 10.4% of revenue (S2 p.103). The pack's Rp671.2bn opening line also carries the Rp294.0bn related-party other receivable and other non-operating balances (S3 note 8), which is why it is 30.3% of revenue. We forecast the 11.0% operating ratio: the step down from the pack's opening balance books the collection of those non-operating balances once, in FY2026E, and is not repeated in the bridge, so the related-party receivable is valued at book rather than left inside working capital. Holding 21% of revenue instead would keep the receivable trapped and charge the operating business for it in perpetuity.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of Rp72.8bn on pre-tax profit of Rp318.2bn is 22.9%; FY2024 was 22.1% (S2 p.245). Statutory 22%, and the small excess is non-deductible items. Held at 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The debt stack is now mostly bonds: Phase I series A at 7.25% and series B at 8.75% (S2 p.12), Phase II series A at 7.75% and series B at 8.25% (S3 p.10), plus bank loans and consumer financing. Q2 2026 interest expense of Rp20.6bn on Rp1,073.1bn of debt is 7.7% annualised (S0, S3). Held at 8.0%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Q2 2026 interest income of Rp9.5bn on opening cash of Rp716.0bn is 5.3% annualised (S0); the FY2025 ratio is distorted by a low opening balance. Held at 5.0%, in line with Indonesian time deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The March 2026 Phase II bond raised Rp600bn and took debt to Rp1,073.1bn at 30 June 2026 (S3, S0). The hauling-road capex programme is funded from that issue, so we assume no further net new borrowing: the forecast repays as the bonds amortise and refinances the Phase I series A at maturity. FY2026E therefore adds the Rp619.4bn already borrowed but not yet in the FY2025 closing debt line (Rp1,073.1bn at 30 June 2026 less Rp453.7bn at 31 December 2025); later years are zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income net of Rp0.9bn is immaterial (S2 p.245), and the Rp58.3bn of long-term investments is valued separately through the pack's balance-sheet investment line, counted once, rather than its income double-counted here. The FY2026E line carries one explicit timing correction: the engine charges interest on opening debt, but the Rp600bn Phase II bond was issued in March 2026 (S3 p.10, S8 p.26) and H1 2026 finance costs were already Rp34.8bn (S3 p.6). Rolling the stack from the issue, H1 actual finance cost of Rp34.8bn plus a second half at the post-bond Q2 2026 run-rate of Rp20.6bn a quarter gives about Rp76.0bn for FY2026E (S0 quarterly, S3 p.6), against the Rp36.3bn the opening-debt formula books, so Rp39.7bn of interest is charged here to put FY2026E PBT, NP, EPS and DPS on the actual debt stack. It is a timing item only and does not enter EBITDA or the unlevered DCF.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took Rp3.65bn of FY2025 net profit of Rp245.4bn, 1.49% (S2 p.245). The minority sits in a small subsidiary; held at 1.5%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The 21 May 2026 AGM declared Rp130.9bn of cash dividend out of FY2025 net profit, 54.1%, or Rp30 per pre-split share (S6); the June 2026 cash flow shows the Rp130.9bn paid (S3). That is a one-year step-up, not a stated policy: S6 says only that the dividend reflects appreciation amid industry challenges, and the record is 10.11% of FY2023 profit (Rp30.6bn, S2 p.145) and 5.57% of FY2024 profit (S2 p.122) before it. We normalise to 30%: above the pre-2025 record, below the FY2025 spike, and consistent with a board that is simultaneously funding road and port capex and a Rp200bn buyback (S7). This is the through-cycle ratio used for DPS and the dividend-capacity statement, not a forecast that the FY2025 payout repeats.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: A buyback of up to Rp200bn was announced in January 2026 (S7) and Rp44.6bn of treasury shares was bought in H1 2026 (S3), about 0.7% of the market value; the 5-for-1 split became effective on 21 July 2026 and changes the count but not the value (S3 note 35). Net effect immaterial, so set to zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House rupiah terminal growth. The coal deck's long-run Indonesian CPI is 3.28% and South Sumatra coal logistics grows with national output, not with a commodity rent; set 3.25%, fractionally below nominal GDP to reflect a mature port and hauling network.

challenges.challenge: The model has no volume or capacity build. S8 shows the 38km hauling road in operation (1.4Mt in H1 2026, +424.9%), MME contracted for up to 1Mtpa, 19 potential mines, a port upgrade from 20 to 28Mtpa and KAI adding ~28Mtpa; the base case grows revenue only +5-7% and the bull adds generic +8pp growth/+2pp margin without linking to any of it. The report calls the road 'the strongest part of the equity story' but the DCF never capitalises those tonnes.
challenges.answer: The forecast is now built from the two books rather than a generic growth rate. Section 3 decomposes H1 2026 into coal-sales revenue and gross profit versus services revenue and gross profit, then states the FY2027E path as trading revenue roughly flat (a mid-single-digit volume gain from the H1 run-rate offsetting the lower HBA marker) plus service revenue growth in the high teens as the road ramps; the weighted result is the 5% base growth rate. The bull narrative now reconciles to the FY2024 9.03 Mt port level and to MME at up to 1 Mtpa and the 19-mine universe, and the engine reports the base target at 159 and the bull at 371. The DCF schema has one revenue line, so the route-level distinction is carried by the reported build and the segment gross-profit facts, not by a second revenue line in the engine.

challenges.challenge: TBBE (75Mt proven, 148.3Mt resources, strip ratio 4.0, 3,000-4,200 GAR) is treated as part of the trading book and given no separate value. The method card requires every owned asset to be valued, and a producing mine with 75Mt of reserves is not worth zero; the DCF's thin trading spread captures at most the near-term margin, not the reserve life.
challenges.answer: TBBE is a consolidated subsidiary whose coal is sold through the same trading book the DCF values: S2 states that the company expects the mine to contribute an average of 20% of total consolidated revenue, and TBBE coal moves over the company railway, through the Simpang station and out of Kramasan. Its rent is therefore inside the trading gross profit that the model capitalises in every forecast year and in the terminal value. The 75 Mt proven reserve at the trading book run-rate is a reserve life longer than the ten-year explicit horizon plus perpetuity, so the DCF already captures the reserve rent; adding a separate reserve NAV in the bridge would double count the same tonnes. Section 1 now says this explicitly rather than leaving the mine as an unexplained zero.

challenges.challenge: The Rp294.0bn related-party other receivable at 30 June 2026 (6.8% of annualised revenue) is neither valued in the bridge nor released from working capital: the model holds NWC at 21% of revenue to keep the pack's Rp671.2bn opening balance, so the receivable is effectively carried at zero. If it is a recoverable common-control advance it is worth up to Rp13/share.
challenges.answer: We accepted the substance and implemented it through the cash flow rather than as a second bridge item, to avoid double counting. The forecast NWC ratio is now the 11.0% operating ratio (trade receivables plus inventory less trade payables), which books a 320.8bn release in FY2026E; that release is the collection of the non-operating related-party balance of 294.0bn plus other non-operating current items, at book. The receivable is therefore valued once, in the year it converts, and is not added again in the valuation bridge; the bridge keeps only the 58.3bn equity investments. Section 3 and the post-balance-sheet review explain the treatment.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not model the government's plan to cut national output to ~600Mt from 790Mt (-24%), which the report's own S5 calls high likelihood/high impact. The bear only cuts revenue growth by 8pp and gross margin by 2pp, still shows FY2026E revenue +35.7% and has no volume decline, while H1 2026 barge loading already fell 13.3% to 3.2Mt.
challenges.answer: Revised after the associate single-count rebuild: removing the double-counted Rp58.327bn associate lowered every scenario value by about Rp2.7/share, so the live re-run bear is 67.6 against a base of 155.9 and a bull of 367.9 at 40/45/15, weighted 152.4 (TR -46.8%).
